newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Peso NDF volume jumps amid post Thailand gloom.
newsitem.headline: Peso NDF volume jumps amid post Thailand gloom.

text.p: Volume in Non Delivery Forwards (NDFs) for the Philippine peso leaped this week, as the spot price came under pressure on speculation of a sharp drop in its value after the Thai baht's float, traders said.

"Volume probably tripled yesterday," said Macer Gifford, global head of NDF trading at Standard Chartered in Singapore. He noted that in the main this did not reflect short selling of the peso, which was stable at 26.399/26.396 on Tuesday.
"So far it's largely been the people who had a yield play on the peso squaring up," he added.

Spot peso came under pressure on Monday after an article in a Sunday Singapore newspaper reported that Philippine finance secretary Roberto de Ocampo said the peso could "devalue" against the U.S. dollar.

Ocampo issued a statement saying he had been misquoted, but a follow-up story issued by the newspaper on Tuesday insisted he was on the record saying there might be 'some kind of devaluation', market forces permitting.
Traders have pondered the idea of a peso depreciation since Thailand was forced to float the baht last week, but its highly regulated forward market is not open to speculators.
A forward market does exist but is only accessible to resident firms for hedging commercial deals. Central bank approval is required for all forward transactions.

This is where NDFs come in, as they allow overseas investors to take forward positions where a price is agreed between a customer and a bank, usually offshore, but settlement on the value date is undertaken entirely in U.S. dollars.
The most liquid currencies in NDF form are the peso, Taiwan dollar and South Korean won, with less turnover in the Indian rupee and Chinese yuan.
While the bulk of trading has been to cover dollar/peso shorts, a few players have taken speculative long dollar/peso positions with traders noting some U.S. interest in that area.
"There has been a lot of hot-money on the peso yield play and that's what's unwinding," said one trader. "There were quite a lot of people who had quite a lot of peso for the yield."

Short term rates have risen to around 30 percent after the Central Bank raised its overnight borrowing rate to that level to defend the peso on Monday. Three month money is currently around 15 or 16 percent.
Despite the rise in NDF volume and the fact that the bulk of the flows are not speculative plays, the impact on the local market will anyway be relatively light, analysts said.

This is because the forward market is more divorced from spot market than was the case of Thailand where the bulk of speculative pressure came from offshore, forcing the Thai central bank to impose capital controls.

"The central bank has made clear that non-deliverable forwards... are against the spirit of 1389. The market is now almost exclusively offshore," said Mark Boyne, treasurer at Hongkong Bank in Manila.
Article 1389 is the Philippine Central Bank's regulation covering foreign exchange.

"But because the Central Bank has made it very clear that NDFs are not an instrument it sees as acceptable and therefore there's no mechanism...by which offshore positions are transferred onshore, it is unlikely (NDFs) will now be able to have a big an influence on the dollar/peso," Boyne said.

Traders in Manila noted repeated rumours that the central bank was looking at whether to further regulate involvement of onshore banks in the NDF market and checking into the accounts of those suspected of doing so.
Nevertheless there is a problem for the peso and while the Philippine economy is unlike Thailand in many ways there are similarities, such as the current account deficit.
"The fundamental issue is that so far they have used hot money flows to plug a hole in the external account," said one trader. "And right now those hot money flows aren't coming through."
"This means they are having to whack up interest rates to try and attract flows back and how long can you sustain that?"
"Thailand managed four months....The peso has just started."
-- Singapore Newsroom +65-870-3091
